lessons.title: CPU, Main Memory and the Fetch-Decode-Execute Cycle

before.content_html:
The Von Neumann Stored-Program Concept

Every computer you have used — from a school laptop to a smartphone — runs on the same fundamental idea: both the program instructions and the data those instructions act on are stored together in the same memory. This is the von Neumann stored-program concept, named after the mathematician John von Neumann, whose work in the 1940s described this model. Before this idea took hold, changing what a computer did meant physically rewiring it. The stored-program concept meant you could change a program simply by changing the data in memory — the same hardware could run any program.

Main memory (RAM) is where instructions and data live while the computer is running. The CPU reads instructions from RAM, processes them, and writes results back. Because RAM is directly accessible by the CPU, it is far faster than any secondary storage device. However, RAM is volatile — everything in it disappears when the power is switched off.

Key Fact

The von Neumann model has five key CPU components: the control unit, the arithmetic logic unit (ALU), registers, the clock, and the three buses (address, data, control). The CPU works directly with main memory (RAM). Every instruction the CPU executes was stored in RAM as data.

Inside the CPU: Components and Their Roles

The control unit does not process data itself. Instead, it orchestrates everything else — sending signals to tell the ALU to calculate, instructing memory to send data, and directing results to the correct destination. During the fetch-decode-execute cycle, the control unit is in charge of every stage.

The ALU is where all computation happens. Arithmetic operations include addition and subtraction. Logical operations include comparisons between values and Boolean operations. Every time a program checks a condition (is the score greater than 50?) or performs a calculation (total price × quantity), the ALU is doing the work.

Registers are tiny storage areas on the processor chip itself. Because they are physically part of the CPU, they can be accessed far faster than RAM. They hold the data that the CPU is working with right now — for example, the result of the last calculation or the address of the next instruction to fetch. You do not need to know the names of specific registers for your exam.

The clock generates a continuous stream of electrical pulses. Each pulse can trigger the start of a new stage in the fetch-decode-execute cycle. The faster the clock, the more stages the CPU can complete per second. A modern CPU typically operates at several gigahertz (GHz) — billions of pulses per second.

A bus is a collection of parallel wires. The CPU communicates with RAM (and other components) via three buses, each carrying a different type of signal:

Address bus — carries the memory address the CPU wants to read from or write to. It is one-directional: the CPU sends addresses out, but nothing sends addresses back to the CPU. The number of address lines determines how many distinct memory locations the CPU can access.

Data bus — carries the actual data or instruction being transferred. It is bidirectional: data travels from RAM to the CPU during a fetch, and from the CPU back to RAM when the CPU writes a result.

Control bus — carries control signals that coordinate the activity of all components. For example, it carries a signal telling RAM whether the current operation is a read (fetch data) or a write (store data). Without the control bus, components would not know when to act or in what direction data should flow.

Together, the three buses make up the system bus — the communication highway between the CPU and main memory.

The Fetch-Decode-Execute Cycle

The CPU operates by endlessly repeating a three-stage process for every instruction in a program. This is the fetch-decode-execute cycle. Each instruction is processed in strict sequence: fetch, then decode, then execute.

Stage 1 — Fetch: The CPU needs to know which instruction to get. It places the address of the next instruction on the address bus. RAM responds by placing the instruction on the data bus. The control bus carries a “read” signal telling RAM that this is a fetch operation, not a write. The instruction arrives at the CPU and is held in a register ready for the next stage.

Stage 2 — Decode: The control unit examines the instruction and works out what operation is required. Different instructions mean different things — one might mean “add two numbers”, another might mean “move data to a different memory location”. The control unit figures out which components need to act and what data they need. No data moves along the buses during decode; this stage happens entirely inside the CPU.

Stage 3 — Execute: The instruction is carried out. If it is an arithmetic operation, the ALU performs the calculation. If data needs to be written to RAM, the CPU places the destination address on the address bus, the data on the data bus, and sends a “write” signal on the control bus. Once execution is complete, the cycle immediately begins again for the next instruction.

This cycle repeats billions of times per second. A common exam error is writing only two stages (“fetch and execute”). There are always three stages: fetch, decode and execute. Omitting decode loses a mark.

Key Fact

During Fetch: the address bus carries the address; the data bus carries the instruction back; the control bus signals a read. During Decode: the control unit interprets the instruction — no bus activity needed. During Execute: the ALU or memory handles the operation; the data bus may carry a result back to RAM via a write signal on the control bus.

Putting It Together: A Worked Example

Imagine a simple program instruction: “Add the value stored at memory address 50 to the value stored at memory address 51 and store the result at address 52.”

Fetch: The address of this instruction (say, address 10) goes out on the address bus. RAM sends the instruction back on the data bus. The control bus signals “read”.

Decode: The control unit reads the instruction. It identifies this as an “add” operation needing two source addresses (50 and 51) and a destination (52). It prepares the ALU.

Execute: The CPU fetches the value at address 50 (using the address bus and data bus), then fetches the value at address 51. The ALU adds them together. The result is placed on the data bus; address 52 goes on the address bus; the control bus signals “write”. RAM stores the result. Cycle complete — on to the next instruction.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The von Neumann stored-program concept means both instructions and data are held together in the same main memory (RAM), allowing the CPU to execute any program stored there.
  • The CPU contains the control unit (manages the cycle), ALU (performs calculations and comparisons), registers (fast on-chip storage), and clock (generates timing pulses). Three buses (address, data, control) connect the CPU to RAM.
  • The fetch-decode-execute cycle has exactly three stages: fetch the instruction from RAM using the buses, decode it in the control unit, then execute it (ALU or memory write). This repeats for every instruction, billions of times per second.

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of the control unit in the fetch-decode-execute cycle.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The control unit manages and coordinates the entire fetch-decode-execute cycle. It sends signals to RAM via the control bus to indicate whether the operation is a read or write. During the decode stage, it interprets the instruction to determine which components must act and what data they need. It then directs the ALU, registers and memory accordingly during execute.
Secure: States the control unit manages the cycle and decodes instructions, with some reference to directing other components.
Developing: States the control unit manages the CPU or decodes instructions, but lacks supporting detail.
Emerging: Vague reference to the control unit being involved in processing.

practice_questions.text: Explain the purpose of the address bus during the fetch stage of the fetch-decode-execute cycle.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: During fetch, the CPU places the address of the next instruction on the address bus. The address bus carries this address to RAM so RAM knows which memory location to access. The address bus is one-directional (CPU to RAM). This allows the correct instruction to be located and placed on the data bus to travel back to the CPU.
Secure: States that the address bus carries the address of the instruction to RAM, with some explanation of why this is needed.
Developing: States the address bus is used during fetch but does not explain its direction or purpose clearly.
Emerging: Names the address bus without explaining its role.

practice_questions.text: State the three stages of the fetch-decode-execute cycle in the correct order.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for all three correct and in order: fetch, decode, execute.

practice_questions.text: Name the component of the CPU that performs arithmetic and logical operations.
Describe what happens during the decode stage of the fetch-decode-execute cycle.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks for: the control unit (1 mark) examines or interprets the instruction to determine what operation is needed and which components must act / what data is required (1 mark). Accept references to the control unit identifying the operation type. No bus activity is required during decode.

practice_questions.text: Discuss whether increasing clock speed is always the best way to improve CPU performance. Consider the role of the clock and other factors that affect performance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies that a higher clock speed means more fetch-decode-execute cycles per second, improving throughput. However, increasing clock speed alone has diminishing returns: it generates more heat, can cause stability issues, and the CPU may still be bottlenecked by RAM access speeds (the bus transfers data at a fixed rate regardless of clock speed). Other factors also affect performance — for example, the number of cores allows parallel processing of independent tasks, and larger on-chip cache reduces the frequency of slow RAM accesses. Concludes that clock speed is one of several factors; the best improvement depends on the workload.
Secure: Identifies clock speed as increasing cycles per second, notes at least one limitation, and mentions one other performance factor (e.g. cores or cache) with some explanation.
Developing: Explains that faster clock means more operations per second; mentions one other factor without development.
Emerging: States clock speed affects performance; little or no development.

before.exam_tip_html: Your exam will test the three stages of the fetch-decode-execute cycle often, sometimes as a 4-mark ‘Describe’ question. Always write all three stages by name and describe what happens in each. Never compress it to ‘fetch and execute’ — examiners look for ‘decode’ as a separate stage. When a question mentions ‘buses’, be specific: name which bus (address, data, or control) and what it carries for that particular step. If asked to ‘Explain’, add the consequence: e.g. “the instruction is placed on the data bus so it can travel from RAM to the CPU.”

Storage questions often ask you to ‘Explain’ which storage type is most suitable for a scenario. Always link your choice to a specific advantage and justify it: don’t just say “SSD is fast” — say “SSD has no moving parts so data is accessed faster, which is important for a laptop that needs to open files quickly on battery power.” For embedded systems, examiners want to see that you understand the fixed-purpose nature: state that the device performs “one specific function” and that the user cannot install new programs.

lessons.title: Operating Systems, Utility Software and Robust Software

before.content_html:
What Is an Operating System?

Every computer needs a layer of software that manages its hardware resources and provides a platform on which applications can run. This is the operating system (OS). Without an OS, every application would need to contain its own code to communicate with hardware — an impossible duplication of effort. Instead, applications request services from the OS, and the OS handles the low-level work.

Your exam requires you to know four specific functions of an operating system: file management, process management, peripheral management and user management. Each addresses a different aspect of running a computer system reliably.

Key Fact

The four OS functions you must know: File management (organising, storing and retrieving files), Process management (deciding which programs get CPU time and when), Peripheral management (handling communication with input/output devices), User management (creating accounts, setting permissions and controlling access).

The Four OS Functions in Detail

File management keeps track of where every file is stored on secondary storage. The OS maintains a directory structure (folders within folders), tracks file names, sizes and locations, and enforces access permissions (who is allowed to read or modify a file). When you save a document, the OS decides where on the storage device to place it and updates its records.

Process management handles multiple programs running at the same time. A modern computer might have dozens of processes active — the browser, the music player, the background virus scan. The OS switches the CPU between them so quickly that they all appear to run simultaneously. It also manages what happens when a process needs to wait (e.g. for a file to load) — pausing that process and giving the CPU to something else.

Peripheral management allows the CPU to communicate with hardware devices such as printers, keyboards, screens and storage devices. Because each device is different, the OS uses a device driver — a small program that translates between the OS’s standard instructions and the specific commands a particular device understands. When you plug in a new printer, the OS loads or downloads the appropriate driver.

User management allows different people to use the same computer with separate settings and access rights. A school network, for example, might allow students to save files only in their own folder and block access to system settings, while giving network administrators full control. Each user has an account with a defined set of permissions.

Utility Software

Utility software carries out maintenance tasks. Unlike application software (which helps users complete their own work), utility programs serve the system itself. The five utility types on your specification are file repair, backup, data compression, disk defragmentation and anti-malware.

File repair — attempts to recover files that have become corrupted or unreadable. This can happen if a drive develops bad sectors, a file is partially overwritten, or a program crashes mid-save. A file repair utility scans for corruption and rebuilds as much of the file as possible.

Backup utility — creates copies of files and stores them in a secondary location (another drive, a network server, or an external device). If the original files are lost or corrupted, they can be restored from the backup. Backup utilities can be scheduled to run automatically so that copies are kept up to date.

Data compression utility — reduces the size of files so they take up less storage space or can be transferred more quickly. Some compression is lossless (the original can be perfectly reconstructed); other compression is lossy (some quality is permanently discarded). A file archiver (such as a ZIP tool) is a common example of lossless compression utility software.

Disk defragmentation — reorganises files on a magnetic hard disk. Over time, as files are added, deleted and modified, their data becomes fragmented — scattered in non-contiguous sections across the disk surface. A defragmenter moves fragments together so the read/write head needs to travel less, speeding up file access. Note: SSDs do not benefit from defragmentation (and it can reduce their lifespan), so this utility applies to magnetic HDDs only.

Anti-malware — detects, quarantines and removes malicious software (malware) such as viruses, spyware and ransomware. It does this by scanning files against a database of known malware signatures, or by monitoring for suspicious behaviour. Anti-malware is a utility because it maintains the health and security of the system rather than performing a user task.

Robust Software: Why It Matters

Robust software is software that continues to work correctly even when things do not go as planned — unexpected inputs, high traffic, or deliberate attempts to exploit a weakness. In safety-critical systems (medical devices, banking, aircraft control), a software failure can have serious real-world consequences. Even in everyday applications, a crash or a vulnerability that leaks user data is costly.

Developing robust software requires identifying vulnerabilities before they can be exploited. Two methods the specification requires you to know are audit trails and code reviews.

A code review is a design-time technique. Before the software is released, one or more developers read through the source code written by a colleague, looking for bugs, logic errors, security weaknesses and poor practices. A fresh pair of eyes often catches vulnerabilities the original developer missed. Code reviews are particularly effective at identifying issues such as missing input validation (which could allow malicious data to crash the program) or hardcoded passwords.

An audit trail is a run-time technique. While the software is in use, it automatically records a timestamped log of significant actions: which user logged in, which files were accessed, what data was changed and when. If a security incident occurs — say, a database record is altered without authorisation — the audit trail provides a record of what happened, when, and under which account. This makes it possible to trace breaches and investigate suspicious activity.

The key distinction: a code review happens before the software runs (during development) and aims to prevent vulnerabilities from shipping. An audit trail happens while the software runs (at runtime) and aims to detect and trace problems after they occur.

Key Fact

A code review is a design-time technique: developers read each other’s source code before release to find bugs and security weaknesses. An audit trail is a run-time technique: the system automatically logs who did what and when, so security breaches can be traced. Code reviews prevent problems; audit trails detect and record them.

practice_questions.text: Name two functions of an operating system.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any two of the four: file management / process management / peripheral management / user management.

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by process management as a function of an operating system.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks for: the OS controls which programs are running at any time (1 mark) and allocates CPU time between them, switching between processes so they appear to run simultaneously (1 mark). Accept references to pausing waiting processes or scheduling.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a code review helps developers create more robust software.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A code review involves one or more developers reading through code written by a colleague before it is released. The reviewer looks for bugs, logic errors, security weaknesses (e.g. missing input validation, hardcoded credentials) and poor coding practices. Because the reviewer did not write the code, they approach it with fresh eyes and can spot issues the original developer overlooked. Identifying vulnerabilities at design time means they can be fixed before users are exposed to them, making the software safer and more reliable.
Secure: States that code review involves another developer checking the code for errors or vulnerabilities before release, with some explanation of why a second perspective is valuable.
Developing: States that a code review involves checking code for errors, without explaining the mechanism or benefit.
Emerging: Vague reference to checking code.

practice_questions.text: Describe the purpose of an audit trail in a software system.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks for: an audit trail is an automatic log (1 mark) that records who performed each action, what was changed, and when, so that security incidents or unauthorised access can be traced or detected (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Explain one difference between a code review and an audit trail as methods of making software more robust.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A code review is a design-time technique carried out before the software is released: developers inspect source code to find and fix vulnerabilities before users encounter them. An audit trail is a run-time technique that operates while the software is live: it logs actions automatically so that if something goes wrong (e.g. a data breach), there is a record of what happened and when. The key difference is timing and purpose: code review prevents problems from shipping; audit trails detect and allow investigation of problems after they occur.
Secure: Identifies that one is before release and one operates during use, with some explanation of each.
Developing: Names both techniques and states one difference without development.
Emerging: Names both techniques with no difference stated.

practice_questions.text: Identify which utility program a system administrator would use if files on a magnetic hard disk were taking much longer to open than usual, and explain why this utility would help.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Disk defragmentation. Over time, files on a magnetic HDD become fragmented — their data is split across non-contiguous sectors of the platter. When a file is opened, the read/write head must physically move to each fragment in turn, increasing access time. Defragmentation reorganises the file data so it is stored in contiguous sectors, meaning the head travels less distance and access is faster. Notes that defragmentation applies to HDDs, not SSDs.
Secure: Identifies defragmentation and explains that fragmented files cause the head to move more, slowing access.
Developing: Identifies defragmentation without a full explanation of why fragmentation causes slowness.
Emerging: Names a utility but incorrect or no explanation.

before.exam_tip_html: When describing OS functions, use precise language — ‘file management’ is not the same as ‘managing the CPU’. Exam questions often give a scenario and ask you to ‘Explain’ which OS function is involved: match the scenario to exactly one of the four functions. For robust software, the key distinction examiners test is design-time vs run-time: code review happens before the software is released; an audit trail runs while the software is live. Always include both the what and the why — don’t just name audit trail, say “it logs user actions so that security breaches can be detected and traced.”

lessons.title: Programming Languages: High-level, Low-level, Compilers and Interpreters

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following correctly describes a compiler?
options: Translates one line of code at a time and stops at the first error
Translates the entire program into machine code before execution and produces a standalone executable
Requires the translator to be present every time the program runs
Is used only for low-level languages

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of programming language uses English-like syntax and can run on different processor types without modification?
Assembly language uses short codes called _____ (e.g. MOV, ADD) to represent machine code instructions.
An interpreter must be present every time the program runs because it does not produce a standalone _____ file.
Match each translator feature to the correct translator:
left: Stops at first error during execution
Produces a standalone machine code file

before.exam_tip_html: The most common exam question on translators is a ‘Describe’ or ‘Explain’ comparing compiler and interpreter. Examiners look for three dimensions: when translation happens (all at once before execution vs line-by-line during execution), what output is produced (standalone executable vs no file), and how errors are handled (all errors listed after analysis vs stops at first error). Don’t just say “a compiler is faster” — explain why: no run-time translation means the executable runs without the overhead of translating each line.
